tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — RHIZOMES PLUS OPEN PANICLE
tiles.details: Look for broad leaves with a pale midrib, but never identify Johnsongrass from a white midrib or purple panicle alone. A real archived Austin-area photograph shows a jointed underground rhizome; trace nodes and connected shoots to distinguish a STEM from a fibrous root. Do not dig, move, or scatter viable invasive rhizome fragments merely to confirm an ID.
tiles.short: Tall warm-season perennial with a 10–50 cm open branched head and creeping scaly underground stems.
tiles.status: REAL RHIZOME PHOTO — SCALE AND AXILLARY BUD DETAIL MISSING

tiles.heading: 02 · OPEN THE TRUE LEAF COLLAR
tiles.details: Peel back the blade at the sheath junction and separate the translucent membrane from its fringe of hairs. The archived Matt Lavin source photo resolves collar hairs, NOT a measurable 2–6 mm membrane edge. Do not draw an arrow to a membrane hidden by the photographed angle; capture a second opened view with a 1-mm ruler.
tiles.short: True ligule is a 2–6 mm membranous flap with a conspicuous ciliate fringe; auricles absent.
tiles.status: COLLAR FRINGE VISIBLE — TRUE MEMBRANE MEASUREMENT MISSING

tiles.heading: 03 · TWO DIFFERENT SPIKELETS FORM A PAIR
tiles.details: At 10–20× trace a short panicle branch to a spikelet without a stalk and its complete stalked companion. The sessile unit usually has bisexual reproductive organs; the pedicelled unit is usually staminate. The sessile spikelet is enclosed by two hardened shiny glumes, while the pedicelled glumes may be thinner. Preserve each attachment in a single photograph with a 1-mm ruler; no existing macro independently establishes the full pair.
tiles.short: Sessile fertile spikelet 3.8–6.5 mm; pedicelled companion 3.6–5.6 mm on a 1.8–3.3 mm stalk.
tiles.status: FNA MEASUREMENTS — ATTACHED PAIRED-SPIKELET MACRO MISSING

tiles.heading: 04 · SEPARATE GLUMES, LEMMAS AND OPTIONAL AWN
tiles.details: Dissect one mature sessile spikelet. Do not confuse the firm shiny OUTER glumes with the thinner INNER lemmas. Kew GrassBase describes a 3.5–5 mm lower sterile lemma and 2–4 mm fertile lemma, sometimes bearing one bent/twisted awn; FNA reports awns absent or up to about 13 mm, while other treatments extend the range. No photograph currently supports a precise awn-origin arrow or species determination from awn length alone.
tiles.short: Sessile glumes enclose the florets; lower sterile lemma about 3.5–5 mm, fertile lemma about 2–4 mm; awn variable.
tiles.status: PUBLISHED ANATOMY — DISSECTED MEASURED LEMMAS MISSING

tiles.heading: 05 · PROTECT NATIVE GRASS LOOK-ALIKES
tiles.details: Sorghastrum nutans has a highly reduced or vestigial pedicelled unit, unlike the developed companion of Sorghum; Panicum virgatum lacks the characteristic sorghum pair. Crop/feral S. bicolor generally lacks extensive creeping scaly rhizomes, but shattercane and hybrids can overlap. Confirm intact spikelets and underground growth before removing a native-looking tall grass; record Sorghum sp. when uncertain.
tiles.short: Native Indiangrass has a strongly reduced pedicelled companion; switchgrass has different small panicle spikelets.
tiles.status: CREW LOOK-ALIKE KEY — MATCHED RIPE MACROS MISSING

tiles.heading: 06 · PUBLIC-READY GATE AND EXACT HANDOFF
tiles.details: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO: same-plant rhizome node and axillary bud with 1-cm scale; opened 2–6 mm ciliate membrane with 1-mm scale; mature attached sessile/pedicelled pair with glumes and detached sterile/fertile lemmas plus actual awn insertion at 10–40×; same-scale Indiangrass, switchgrass and grain-sorghum comparisons. NEEDS_SITE_QA: verify all ten original photo records, per-photo rights/attribution, existing and newly recorded visible-only gross arrows, physical JPEG integrity, and public mobile rendering. Preserve introduced/invasive comparison status and all original taxonomy/range holds; do not mark FINISHED.
tiles.short: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS — useful rhizome and collar photos exist; paired-spikelet anatomy is still unproven.

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: JOHNSONGRASS (INTRODUCED, INVASIVE): rather tall PERENNIAL Sorghum with broad flat leaves sometimes showing pale white midrib and often an OPEN purplish panicle. Neither color nor a white midrib proves ID. STRONG CONFIRMATION is long, creeping, jointed SCALY UNDERGROUND RHIZOMES with root-bearing nodes, seen in the existing actual Austin source photo. A true collar photo shows a fringe of hairs at the membranous ligule region (membrane length not measured). Fertile sessile spikelet plus companion pedicelled unit needs an intact mature macro. Don't dig or transport viable rhizome fragments unnecessarily.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: Perennial C4 warm-season coarse grass, usually robust upright culms from an underground branching rhizome system; colonies expand from both seed and vegetative buds.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: Peel back the blade at the sheath junction and separate the translucent membrane from its fringe of hairs. The archived Matt Lavin source photo resolves collar hairs, NOT a measurable 2–6 mm membrane edge. Do not draw an arrow to a membrane hidden by the photographed angle; capture a second opened view with a 1-mm ruler.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: Large loose open 10–50(-55) cm branched terminal panicle, 5–25 cm wide (FNA/GrassBase); primary branches divided into short paired-spikelet-bearing raceme units. May be purplish at flowering, straw colored at maturity.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

panels.label: NATIVE LOOK-ALIKE · Indiangrass actual collar and projecting ligule
panels.caption: This is NATIVE Indiangrass (Sorghastrum nutans), not Johnsongrass. Matt Lavin's real ligule/sheath photo documents its characteristic projecting membranous 'rifle sight' appearance. Compare the same leaf junction in Johnsongrass rather than deciding from flower color. Johnsongrass itself also has a membranous, ciliate ligule; differences require interpreting the entire collar and plant.

panels.label: NATIVE LOOK-ALIKE · Indiangrass fertile spikelet, bent awn and bare pedicels
panels.caption: Actual Indian grass macro by Matt Lavin. A fertile spikelet bears a conspicuous bent/twisted awn, beside NAKED pedicels where the neighboring pedicelled spikelet is strongly reduced. Johnsongrass instead typically retains distinct developed sessile and pedicelled spikelet members in pairs. This is a close-up of the NATIVE comparator, never label its spikelet as a Johnsongrass unit.

panels.label: INTRODUCED LOOK-ALIKE · Grain sorghum attached panicles and broad blades
panels.caption: Grain sorghum (Sorghum bicolor), an introduced crop/escape, has broad blades and a variable, sometimes dense, flowering head. These flowering shoots alone are not enough to decide species: wild Johnson grass is a persistent rhizomatous perennial whereas grain sorghum is commonly annual and non-rhizomatous. Verify roots only where collecting is lawful and do not identify by cultivated setting alone.

intro: JOHNSONGRASS (INTRODUCED, INVASIVE): rather tall PERENNIAL Sorghum with broad flat leaves sometimes showing pale white midrib and often an OPEN purplish panicle. Neither color nor a white midrib proves ID. STRONG CONFIRMATION is long, creeping, jointed SCALY UNDERGROUND RHIZOMES with root-bearing nodes, seen in the existing actual Austin source photo. A true collar photo shows a fringe of hairs at the membranous ligule region (membrane length not measured). Fertile sessile spikelet plus companion pedicelled unit needs an intact mature macro. Don't dig or transport viable rhizome fragments unnecessarily.
memory_rule: JOHNSONGRASS (EXOTIC): often prominent WHITE MIDRIB + broad leaves, open panicle, developed paired sessile/pedicelled spikelets, long jointed creeping rhizomes. INDIANGRASS (NATIVE): prominent rifle-sight collar, bent-awn fertile spikelet and naked reduced companion pedicel. GRAIN SORGHUM (EXOTIC crop): often annual without creeping rhizomes. Do not identify or remove from one trait alone.
safety_note: Ten existing exact-species local photo records, but only five were in the canonical visual gallery before this lane-2 pass. Three more real source images connected without inventing pixel arrows. Rhizome bud locations, ligule membrane length, paired spikelet measurements and live Pages QA remain unverified.
field_rule: The physically photographed creeping segmented rhizome is the strongest Johnsongrass-versus-grain-sorghum cue; complete attached spikelet pairs and true ligule measurements remain absent.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.

morphology.habit: Perennial C4 warm-season coarse grass, usually robust upright culms from an underground branching rhizome system; colonies expand from both seed and vegetative buds.
morphology.inflorescence: Large loose open 10–50(-55) cm branched terminal panicle, 5–25 cm wide (FNA/GrassBase); primary branches divided into short paired-spikelet-bearing raceme units. May be purplish at flowering, straw colored at maturity.
